rule.summary: A quote or paraphrase attributed to a named source must preserve its actual meaning and degree of certainty; amplifying a conditional warning into a definite criminal outcome is the kind of meaning-change that undermines the channel's diligence defense (Masson) and draws extra platform scrutiny for civic/election-adjacent claims.

issues.excerpt: DOJ: knowingly count ballots, face charges
issues.scenario: F13's actual DOJ quote is conditional ('opening themselves to legal jeopardy'); the bold on-screen hook text attributed to 'DOJ' instead asserts a definite outcome DOJ did not state. This is the first thing viewers read -- not softened narration, which is why I keep this at high rather than medium. A critic, a later-cleared official, or a platform fact-checker could point to this as the channel putting a stronger claim in DOJ's mouth than DOJ made, inside the 10-day pre-election window platforms police for civic-integrity claims.

rule.summary: Attribution must be precise about who said what and in what role; the dossier itself keeps Logan's group (L2, election administrators) and DeSaulnier's group (L3, congressional Democrats) separate because their standing and arguments differ.

issues.excerpt: California election officials disagree. LA County Registrar Dean Logan called the new letters a 'posture of intimidation.' Rep. Mark DeSaulnier called it 'the escalating weaponization of the Justice Department.'
issues.scenario: The lead-in 'California election officials disagree' is immediately followed by a quote from Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, a sitting member of Congress, not an election administrator. A sharp viewer, fact-checker, or DeSaulnier's office could flag the mislabeling as inaccurate role attribution in an election-sensitive story, which platforms actively police for unverified claims about an election.

rule.summary: Format.md requires a separate music-less YouTube mix for any cut longer than 60s, because YouTube blocks Shorts 61-90s outright on any active Content ID claim 'regardless of policy' (platforms/youtube/rules.md §6), and CC0 tracks here have unknown Content ID status.

issues.excerpt: script_team.json music block: {enabled: true, duration_s: 90, one cue spanning the full runtime} with no YouTube-specific no-music variant noted; music/catalog.yaml lists content_id: unknown for every approved CC0 track.
issues.scenario: If the rendered YouTube Short keeps the same music track as the TikTok/Instagram cuts and any rights holder (or a library that registered the CC0 track in Content ID without the channel's knowledge) files a claim, YouTube auto-blocks the entire Short on that platform -- not just demonetizes it -- regardless of the track's CC0 licensing. I keep this at high rather than platform_report's medium: the realistic worst case here is a full removal of the upload, not a reach or revenue hit, given every candidate track's Content ID status is unknown.

rule.summary: Cover art must stay in the channel's own pixel-art brand and state only what's in the dossier; it should not borrow real institutional insignia that could make the thumbnail read as official or affiliated content, the pattern YouTube's thumbnail/misleading-metadata policy cautions against.

issues.excerpt: Stylized California map with a pulsing red alert over a ballot-box icon and a small DOJ seal stamp in the corner.
issues.scenario: A viewer or a platform reviewer doing a quick thumbnail check could read the DOJ seal as implying the video is official DOJ content or produced with the agency's involvement. None of the three platforms' rules carve out an exception for stylized government insignia on an unaffiliated news channel's cover, so this is a precautionary edit rather than a clear violation.

rule.summary: Format.md explicitly bans pairing tense music, dark lighting or 'villain framing' with a real person who has not been found guilty of anything, stating that combination is itself an accusation; the dossier's own risk list separately bars dramatized arrest, crime, or endorsement scenes for any named official.

issues.excerpt: A sealed thumb drive with a padlock icon sits untouched on a county office desk; nearby, Secretary Weber signs a letter at her own desk as a calendar flips its pages from Oct 13 to Oct 27 and a gavel icon appears. -- shown under the episode's tense chiptune cue, described as building through 'what's-new' and 'known' and lifting at points through the runtime.
issues.scenario: Weber is the California official refusing to hand DOJ the password-protected list and contesting DOJ's lawsuit -- she is not accused of any crime, and the Oct. 27 hearing is about the county's refusal to comply, not about her personal conduct. Placing a gavel icon directly over her shot, under the episode's building tense score, visually suggests she personally faces judgment for that hearing -- the exact visual-plus-score 'verdict' framing format.md forbids for anyone not yet adjudicated. Weber's office, or a platform civil-integrity reviewer doing a frame-by-frame check in the pre-election window, could read this as implying an unresolved legal conclusion about a named election official that the narration itself never states.
